evidence.label: Tensor saturation for even spin groups

headline: For even spin groups, an invariant after stretching the weights implies one before, if the weights pass a parity test.
scope: The claim covers Spin(2n) for every n of 2 or more, the type D case. Other simply laced types, E6, E7 and E8, are not covered.
plain: Combining three symmetry patterns of a group sometimes leaves something unchanged, called an invariant. The saturation question asks whether, if stretched versions of the patterns combine to an invariant, the originals do too. A simple parity test is needed, and Knutson and Tao settled the question for one family in 1999. This paper claims to settle it for the even spin groups, called type D.
doesNot: This does not cover the exceptional simply laced groups E6, E7 and E8.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Misha Kapovich and John Millson, “Structure of the tensor product semigroup”
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles the type D part of a conjecture whose type A case was a celebrated 1999 theorem.

explanation:
Start with the simplest symmetry group in this story, SL(2). Its basic representations are labelled by whole numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. Combining labels a and b gives the labels from |a − b| up to a + b, in steps of 2. Three representations a, b, c combine to leave something unchanged when c appears in a combined with b.

Try 1, 1, 1. Combining 1 and 1 gives 0 and 2, but not 1. So there is no invariant. Now stretch everything by 2, to get 2, 2, 2. Combining 2 and 2 gives 0, 2 and 4, which includes 2. Now there is an invariant. Stretching created one where none existed. The reason is parity: 1 + 1 + 1 is odd, while 2 + 2 + 2 is even.

So any honest version of the question needs a parity test. In general this test asks that the three labels add up to an element of the root lattice[2]. The root lattice is the set of labels that the group's basic directions, its roots, can reach. Without it, the group's center acts and kills any invariant[2]. For SL(2), the test is that a + b + c is even.

The saturation problem asks this. If stretched labels give a tensor invariant, do the original labels give one too[1]? A tensor invariant here is a vector in the combined representation that the whole group leaves fixed. The question links to the geometry of eigenvalues, through work of Klyachko[14]. Knutson and Tao answered it for type A, the groups SL(n), with their honeycomb theorem in 1999[3]. Kapovich and Millson then conjectured the same, with the parity test, for all simply laced groups[4].

Before this paper, type D was known only in small cases. Kapovich, Kumar and Millson did Spin(8)[8]. Kiers did Spin(10) and Spin(12). Other work showed that a stretch by four always suffices for these groups. Those results do not give the factor-one statement under the parity test[9].

This paper claims the type D case[5]. For Spin(2n) with n at least 2, three labels that pass the parity test give an invariant whenever some stretch of them does[6]. The claim includes the half-integer spin labels[7]. For n = 2, Spin(4) is two copies of SL(2), so the opening example is a piece of it.

The proof turns the question into one about paths through the space of labels. Real-number paths exist by a geometric argument. The one obstacle is making them integral. The directions used may span the space without reaching every lattice point[10]. In type D the paper shows only one obstruction remains, a parity mismatch between two pieces[11]. It moves the path to fix that mismatch, while keeping the path admissible throughout[13]. A separate construction then turns integral paths into actual invariants[12].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper. The claim rests on the paper's own long argument. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proof holds. No Lean check is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A way for a group to act on a vector space by linear maps.
The label that picks out one irreducible representation of the group.
A vector in a combined (tensor product) representation that every group element leaves fixed.
The set of labels reachable by whole-number combinations of the group's roots.
The property that an invariant after stretching the labels implies one before.
A group that double-covers the rotations of a space; Spin(2n) is type D.
